USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Continue the current negotiating track and preserve the 90-day truce, pressing for enforceable commitments on IP protection and forced technology transfer while keeping the March 2 tariff-hike to 25% on the $200B list as a credible backstop. Do not escalate (raising tariffs, entity-listing Huawei, or letting the Meng extradition poison the talks), and do not concede structural gains yet — hold the leverage and convert the goodwill concessions China is already offering into a durable, verifiable agreement.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat reading is mildly favorable-to-opportunity (-0.25), not high, because the US enters 10 January 2019 with the stronger hand. The Beijing talks (Jan 7-9) were extended beyond schedule to a third day, the US delegation called them constructive, and Trump reported 'Talks with China are going very well' (web_search, CNBC/Reuters 2019-01-08/09). China has delivered concrete goodwill concessions — successive large soybean purchases and long-awaited approvals to import five GM crops that boost US grain exports (Reuters 2019-01-08). The G20 truce deferred the threatened January 1 tariff increase, keeping escalation on US terms (event_timeline 2018-12-01, 2019-01-07). This matches the -0.5 USA anchor of 'leverage to extract concessions' but is tempered toward neutral because the dispute is visibly biting markets and sentiment: the S&P 500 has fallen about 8% since the truce, the 10-year Treasury yield has slid from ~3.2% to ~2.7%, UMich consumer sentiment dropped to 91.2 in January from 98.3, and Baa credit spreads have widened to ~5.13% (country_health, USA series). The Huawei/Meng extradition and Beijing's detention of two Canadians (event_timeline 2018-12-10) create a second, security-linked escalation track that could easily spill into the trade talks and strain allied (Canada) cohesion (web_search, CBS/NYT 2018-12). These cross-currents argue against escalation — the environment is too fragile — but the leverage argument argues against concession, so the disciplined stance is negotiate/hold at 0.0 while converting China's willingness to buy into enforceable structural change before the March 2 deadline.
key_factors: US holds negotiating leverage and is extracting concrete concessions (soybean purchases, GM crop approvals, extended talks)
90-day truce defers tariff escalation to March 2, keeping leverage on US terms
Markets and sentiment fragile: S&P -8% since truce, 10y yield to ~2.7%, UMich sentiment to 91.2, Baa spreads ~5.1%
Huawei/Meng extradition + detained Canadians create a separate security track that could spill into and derail trade talks
Structural issues (IP, forced tech transfer, enforcement) remain unresolved and far apart

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Continue the constructive negotiating path opened at the G20 truce — hold our tariff posture unchanged, signal willingness to increase purchases of US agricultural/energy goods, and push for a settlement before the March 1 deadline rather than escalating. Avoid new retaliatory measures that would deepen damage to our already-strained export sector, and keep the Huawei/Meng file separate from the trade track to avoid torpedoing talks.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to China is high — tariffs now cover ~$250B of our exports at 10-25%, the Huawei/Meng arrest signals firm-level tech-supply targeting, and the real economy is already decelerating: November industrial production fell to 5.4% (its lowest since 2009), Q3 GDP was 6.5% (slowest since 2009), export growth halved, the RMB depreciated ~6% and equities lost ~20% (World Bank/Dec 2018 trade data). That justifies a +0.5 high-banded threat score. But it is not existential: we retain stimulus headroom (PBoC liquidity, fiscal/infrastructure), large reserves, and an active truce with talks that resumed Jan 7-8. Critically, the US is also under visible strain (consumer sentiment tumbled to 91.2, the 10Y yield fell from ~3.1 to 2.56, oil crashed to ~$46-52, credit spreads widened), so the terrain favors reaching a deal rather than escalation. Because our export economy is more exposed than the US to further tariff escalation, the rational stance is de-escalatory engagement that buys time and extracts a fair settlement, not retaliation: action_score +0.1, negotiate.
key_factors: US Section 301 tariffs now cover ~$250B of Chinese exports (List1/2 @25%, List3 @10%)
Dec 1 G20 truce suspended the Jan 1 hike to 25%; hard March 1 deadline; talks resumed Jan 7-8 Beijing

Real economy already decelerating: Nov IP growth 5.4% (lowest since 2009), GDP 6.5% (slowest since 2009), exports halved, RMB ~-6%, equities ~-20%
China has policy headroom: PBoC liquidity, infrastructure and fiscal stimulus being deployed
US itself under strain (sentiment 98.3->91.2, 10Y 3.08->2.56, oil 75->46), giving China negotiating leverage
